title: AI Software That Can Change The Horse Racing Industry
summary:
We didn’t believe that there would be a time when we would talk about artificial intelligence technology entering the traditional world of horse racing, yet here we are. This means that AI is literally everywhere, and there isn’t a single industry that’s left unimpacted by this technology, either directly or indirectly, and for the better or worse. And as it seems, it is already changing the horse racing industry in many different ways. Ways that we didn’t imagine will change for centuries. But before you get all excited about having an AI superbot that will accurately predict the winner of a race, that’s not the case here. Horse racing is still a very unpredictable sport, and even AI with mountains of data cannot figure out which horse is going to win. So, no, AI didn’t ruin betting. The thing that AI is changing in the horse racing industry is safety, analytics, data collection, automation, and making everything easier to manage.

Sleip Can Turn an iPhone Into a Gait-Analysis Tool

The best way to explain the AI change in the horse racing industry is to see what’s already happening in the sport. That way we can get a vague idea of what it will look like in the future. One of the best examples is Sleip, which is a Swedish equine tech company using computer vision to analyze how horses move. We’re talking about a remarkably simple idea, yet it has the power to change the entire industry. You basically record your horse trotting with your phone, upload the video, and then the app uses artificial intelligence with more than 100 anatomical points to measure subtle asymmetries in areas including the head, withers, and pelvis. The tech can spot even the slightest imperfections that are impossible for trainers to see with the naked eye. However, this isn’t a diagnostic tool; let’s get that thing straight. It is a technology that measures movement and provides objective information so professional vets can interpret alongside their normal examination. For racehorses, longitudinal monitoring may be particularly valuable. Sleip's Trends feature allows users to compare gait measurements over time, creating an individual baseline for each horse rather than judging every recording in isolation. The company says trainers and regulators, including organizations connected with Hong Kong, Britain, Australia, and New York racing, have increasingly used this type of longitudinal gait information around training and pre-race assessment. A trainer who sees the same horse every morning already develops an extraordinary eye for tiny changes. When you think about it, even fans can use this app. Imagine you’re attending the Breeders’ Cup, and you record the horses before they get behind the starting gate, put them through the app, and it will tell you their advantages and disadvantages, or problems they face. Yes, some might say a misuse of the tech’s power, but we don’t do any harm, right? Any data in horse racing betting is valuable, but before you place a bet, make sure you claim the horse racing sign up bonus by TwinSpires, just to be safe.

StrideSAFE Is Looking for Trouble Before It Becomes Obvious

Another fascinating system is StrideSAFE. Instead of analyzing smartphone video, StrideSAFE uses a lightweight sensor placed in the saddle cloth while a Thoroughbred races. The system records gait and motion data at high frequency, then uses algorithms developed from a growing database of racing performances to identify horses whose movement patterns may warrant closer veterinary attention. As of 2026, StrideSAFE says the technology has collected data from more than 75,000 starts and is deployed at tracks across Kentucky as well as Belmont and Saratoga. Its software is designed to identify movement patterns associated with risks such as condylar and sesamoid fractures, providing reports that trainers and veterinarians can review after racing. That could become one of the most important uses of AI in the entire sport.

Arioneo Wants to Understand the Entire Athlete

Where Sleip concentrates heavily on movement analysis, Arioneo is building something closer to an equine performance ecosystem. Its EQUIMETRE systems combine sensor data with software capable of analyzing heart rate, ECG, speed, locomotion, and recovery during training. Arioneo says its AI models are trained on billions of equine data points and can automatically interpret sessions, recognize exercise types, and benchmark a horse against comparable data. This matters because trainers already collect a great deal of information. The problem is turning it into something useful. A horse might record a particular speed during morning work, but speed alone says very little. How hard was the cardiovascular effort required to produce it? How quickly did the horse recover? Did stride frequency change? Was the work more demanding than a similar session three weeks earlier? Arioneo's platform is designed to put those signals together rather than treating each number separately. The company now also offers an AI-based vision app that tracks 31 key points on a horse from ordinary video and estimates locomotor asymmetry.

AI Could Also Make Heart Monitoring More Practical

Cardiac data is another promising area. Arioneo's newer racing system is designed to collect ECG and locomotion data while horses are actually competing rather than only during controlled training. Its software can automatically screen recordings for arrhythmias and generate reports for trainers, veterinarians, and racing institutions. That is a significant change. Traditionally, gathering high-quality ECG data during maximum-intensity racing has been technically difficult. A horse galloping flat out under race conditions is not exactly volunteering for a relaxed cardiology appointment. Software capable of processing those recordings at scale could help researchers understand what happens to the equine heart during genuine racing effort rather than relying entirely on laboratory or training conditions.

AI Could Change Breeding Too, but This Is Where Caution Matters

Breeding is another area where machine learning will inevitably attract attention. The industry already has enormous databases containing pedigrees, race records, surfaces, distances, and performance histories. In theory, AI could identify combinations of bloodlines associated with particular racing traits or compare prospective matings across far more variables than a human could comfortably process.

Final Thoughts

The sport is already changing, and with this fast rate of advancements in the world of AI, things are changing really quickly. The good news is that AI is currently centering on safety and analytics, but soon the tech will touch things like experience, convenience, and many other segments.
ja_summary:
AI技術が競馬界に導入され、歩様分析や心拍計測による馬の健康管理・安全性の向上が進んでいる。
スマホ動画やセンサーで取得した膨大なデータをAIが解析し、肉眼では困難な故障の予兆検知や運動能力の客観的評価を可能にした。

title: The Combinator Pattern: Elegant Composition for Modern Python Developers
summary:
As software systems evolve, their business logic often becomes increasingly complex. Logic that initially seems simple gradually gets embedded in classes and entities, making the code harder to maintain, extend, and reuse. Every new requirement may force developers to modify existing implementations, increasing complexity and the risk of introducing defects.

The Combinator Design Pattern offers an elegant way to address these challenges. Instead of implementing complex logic as tightly coupled control flow, we can represent individual rules as independent, first-class functions and compose them to construct more sophisticated behavior.

This presentation explores the Combinator Pattern from both theoretical and practical perspectives, showing how Python's support for first-class functions enables flexible, reusable software components.

We begin by reviewing first-class objects in Python and the role of design patterns in solving recurring software development problems. We then examine common design challenges, including business logic accumulating within entities and the difficulties that arise when requirements change.

Using password validation as a practical example, we show how you can define individual validation rules independently and combine them into more complex validation policies. Rather than hardcoding validation logic inside a class, we can assemble the required behavior from reusable building blocks.

The presentation also examines how the Combinator Pattern supports fundamental object-oriented design principles:

- Single Responsibility Principle (SRP): Separating individual logic units from the entities that use them, improving separation of concerns.
- Open-Closed Principle (OCP): Allowing developers to introduce new combinations of behavior without modifying existing logic units.
- Code Maintainability: Making implementations easier to understand, extend, and maintain by organizing logic into small, reusable components.

One of the central messages of this presentation is that complex software behavior does not necessarily require complex implementations. By modeling logic as composable units, developers can create flexible solutions that adapt more easily to changing requirements.

The Combinator Pattern demonstrates how thoughtful software design can simplify development while improving code quality and maintainability.

These slides are intended for Python developers, software architects, and anyone interested in design patterns, functional composition, and building cleaner, more maintainable software.

More information about this talk and the code samples it uses can be found at https://lifemichael.com/en/exploring-the-combinator-pattern-at-python-summit-2026/
